title: Eighteen schools
hookLine: the early schools multiplied, each with its own reading of the texts

cards: Eighteen. That's the number the old chronicles give for the schools that grew up after the first split. The trouble is, when you put the lists side by side, they don't name the same eighteen.

Some lists have more names than that. Some schools appear under two names. The number stays the same while the names shift around it, as if eighteen were less a count than a way of saying: a whole family of schools.

teach.b: These weren't separate religions. A school, a nikaya, was a community of monks with its own lineage, its own copy of the discipline, and often its own way of reading the teaching.
A few of the readings: the Sarvastivada taught that all things exist in the past, present and future, and their name is read as those who say all exists.
Another family of schools, the Pudgalavadins, held that there is a person, a pudgala, which is neither the same as the parts of body and mind nor separate from them.

teach.h: ALL EXISTS, A PERSON, BEYOND THE WORLD.
teach.b: The Lokottaravada, a branch of the great community, taught that the Buddha's life in the world was in a deep sense beyond the world. The Theravada called itself the teaching of the elders. How did they argue?
The Theravada canon even contains a book, the Kathavatthu, that sets out points of controversy as question and answer: a position is stated, questioned, and answered.
It is written from the Theravada side, but it preserves the questions other schools were asking.
Today the Theravada continues as a living school with its canon in Pali, and the discipline codes of other early schools still guide monks and nuns in East Asia and Tibet.
Each of these schools kept faith with the texts the way its teachers had, and each, the Theravada included, understood itself as keeping the Buddha's teaching whole.

how: Buddhist monastics today are ordained in lineages whose discipline codes trace back to particular early schools, and students of Buddhism read the early schools' debates in texts like the Kathavatthu.

games.q: you're a monk in the early schools, and the monastery down the road reads a teaching differently. what do the old texts show monks doing?
o: refusing to speak with the other monks.
setting out the points as question and answer.
games.why: the Kathavatthu states each position, questions it and answers it. the debates were recorded, not hidden.

practice: Think of a text, a family saying or even a recipe that you and someone else read differently, and say their reading to yourself as fairly as you can.
Then find one thing in it you can respect, what it protects or what it notices that yours might miss.

wordCard.voice: Eighteen schools. The chronicles' name for the early schools that grew from the first split, each with its own reading of the teaching. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: a group or collection; used both for a school of monks and for a collection of suttas.

carryVoice: Your line: many readings. Eighteen was less a count than a family. See you tomorrow.
